book_title: The Alchemy of My Mortal Form
subject_line: A poem for each of Arkansas's 52 state parks
email_body:
Dear Sandy,

I read the December 2025 profile describing your 52 Parks: 52 Poems project, written for the centennial of Arkansas State Parks, and it struck me as a long way from the single sickly speaker of The Alchemy of My Mortal Form, the persona sequence that won the Louise Bogan Award. I would love to ask how you approached a park you had little personal history with, and whether moving between fifty-two places changed how you think about the place-based poems of Blood Almanac.

subject_line: Solace from the Northwoods, on the page and on film
email_body:
Dear Patricia,

I saw that Solace: Poems from the Northwoods was chosen by Diane Seuss for the Summit Series Prize for Michigan Writers and is coming out from Central Michigan University Press. Your NMU page also describes you as a poetry filmmaker, which made me curious about how the two practices meet. Do any of the Northwoods poems begin as images or footage before they become lines, and does the Upper Peninsula landscape ask something different of a poem than of a film?

subject_line: From The Snowbound House to The First Echo
email_body:
Dear Shane,

Looking at your three collections side by side, from The Snowbound House and its Philip Levine Prize, through the Hollis Summers Prize winner The Surface of the Lit World, to The First Echo from LSU Press, I noticed how each title holds a kind of threshold: a house, a surface, a first sound coming back. I would like to ask whether you see those books as one continuing conversation, and how directing the MFA program at UMSL has shaped what you are writing.

book_title: The Book of Fools: An Essay in Memoir and Verse
subject_line: An essay in memoir and verse: The Book of Fools
email_body:
Dear Sam,

The subtitle of The Book of Fools, An Essay in Memoir and Verse, caught my attention on your Wichita State faculty page. After Body of the World and Nude Descending an Empire, it reads like a deliberate step outside the shape of a poetry collection. I would like to ask what the fool figure let you say about your own life that a lyric speaker could not, and how you decided where the prose should give way to verse.

subject_line: The "vs." in tsunami vs. the fukushima 50
email_body:
Dear Lee Ann,

The title of tsunami vs. the fukushima 50, your Milkweed collection, sets up a contest between a wave and the workers who stayed behind at the plant, and that small "vs." has stayed with me. Coming after Dandarians, it feels like a book that pushes outward from the personal toward catastrophe. I would like to ask how you found the voice for a force of nature, and whether editing South Dakota Review from Vermillion changes how you read disaster writing from far away.

subject_line: From The Lengest Neoi toward Wherever Shore
email_body:
Dear Stephanie,

I came to The Lengest Neoi through the news that Brenda Shaughnessy chose it for the 2023 Iowa Poetry Prize, and then read about your 2025 Hargis Fellowship at Oklahoma State's Doel Reed Center. The description of your next project, Wherever Shore, and its documentary approach to Chinese American histories, made me curious about that turn toward the archive. How do you decide when a found record should stay intact on the page, and when it needs your own voice around it?

subject_line: Between An Image Not a Book and Name & Earth
email_body:
Dear Kylan,

Reading the titles of An Image Not a Book from 2023 and Name & Earth this year, I noticed how they talk to each other: the first refuses to be a book, the second sets a word beside the ground it might stand for. I would like to ask whether that tension between naming and the actual land is something you carried consciously from one book to the next, and how teaching in Logan has entered the new poems.

I would like to ask what toughness means in the new poems, and whether Reno and the Great Basin are as present in it as in the earlier books.

subject_line: Spokane Falls, 1889, and the fire nobody can explain
email_body:
Dear Leyna,

In your Rumpus interview with Aileen Keown Vaux, I was struck by how Fire Season began: while you were working as a Spokane tour guide, drawn to the fact that no one knows how the 1889 fire started. You also said many of the strangest details in the book are true. I would like to ask how you decided where the historical record ends and your fabulism takes over, and what that line looks like in the new story collection.

subject_line: Hematology, Body Parts, and the body on the page
email_body:
Dear Kristin,

On your University of Southern Indiana faculty page I noticed how closely your two titles sit together: the full-length collection Hematology, which won the 2021 Harbor Editions Laureate Prize, and the chapbook Body Parts. Both name the body in almost clinical terms. I would like to ask where that vocabulary of blood and anatomy first entered your poems, and whether writing Hematology changed the way you return to the poems in Body Parts.
